questions.q: What are the two main components of setting in a poem, and give one example of each from the first stanza of "ljkst Le`fr"?
questions.a: The two main components are time and place. In the first stanza, time is "evening" (fookg, vkewy uoy) and place is the "riverbank" (rq>) with a "dense forest of tall trees" ('kqHk iM+k dy'k). A wrong answer like "characters and plot" reveals the student confuses setting with narrative elements and cannot distinguish the spatiotemporal framework from the story.

questions.q: In the line "gksBksa esa fctyh i¡Qlh Lian" (in the laps, a sleeping child), the poet uses a metaphor. Explain how this metaphor transforms the physical setting into an emotional atmosphere.
questions.a: The metaphor "gksBksa" (laps) personifies nature (the forest/riverbank) as a nurturing mother holding the child. This transforms the physical setting from a mere location into a protective, maternal embrace, creating an atmosphere of safety, tenderness, and organic unity between human life and nature. A wrong answer that only identifies "child sleeping" without explaining the personification shows the student misses how setting becomes emotionally charged through figurative language.

questions.a:
1. "rq> ij 'kqHk iM+k dy'k dk ty" (on the bank, a dense forest of tall trees) — visual; creates enclosure, protection, intimacy.  
2. "gksBksa esa fctyh i¡Qlh Lian" (in the laps, a sleeping child) — visual/tactile; creates tenderness, vulnerability, peace.  
3. "mj esa Hkj >wyh Nfc lqanj" (in it, a very beautiful star shines) — visual; adds wonder, quiet beauty, a focal point in the darkening sky.  
A wrong answer listing images without linking each to a distinct atmospheric quality (e.g., just "it shows nature") reveals the student cannot differentiate how specific sensory details layer to build a complex mood.

questions.q: Compare the setting in the first stanza (present riverbank evening) with the setting implied in the memory stanza ("os gh lq[k&nq[k esa jgs U;Lr" — they used to stay in that very small cradle). How does the shift in setting alter the atmosphere?
questions.a: The first stanza is an open, natural, present-moment setting (riverbank, forest, star) creating a serene, expansive atmosphere. The memory stanza shifts to a domestic, enclosed, past setting (wooden cradle "Lusg&xksn", parents' lap "ekek&ekeh dk jgk I;kj") creating a cozy, nostalgic, intergenerational atmosphere. The shift moves the atmosphere from immediate sensory peace to layered emotional continuity — the speaker now occupies the mother's role, and the setting bridges generations. A wrong answer that treats both stanzas as the same setting misses the temporal and spatial shift that deepens the poem's emotional architecture.

questions.q: The poem ends with the speaker praying: "bl iFk ij] esjs dk;Z ldy gksa Hkz"V 'khr osQ&ls 'krny!" (at this very point, may my work be finished, away from the hard moments!). Evaluate how the riverbank evening setting makes this prayer more poignant.
questions.a: The evening setting is inherently transitional — it moves inevitably toward night. This natural temporality mirrors the speaker's awareness that the perfect moment of motherhood (the child sleeping, the memory merging) is fleeting. The setting's beauty and peace make the desire to freeze time universal and heartbreaking. The prayer is not just personal; it is spoken against a backdrop that embodies impermanence. A wrong answer that calls the prayer "sad" without referencing the setting's inevitable progression (evening → night) fails to evaluate the interplay between external environment and internal longing.

questions.q: Write a 4-line stanza describing a setting that creates an atmosphere of anxious waiting, using at least three distinct sensory details (visual, auditory, olfactory/tactile).
questions.a:
Example:  
The corridor hums with fluorescent glare, (visual)  
Clock ticks like a heartbeat in sterile air. (auditory)  
Antiseptic sting in each breath I take, (olfactory/tactile)  
Shadows stretch — how much longer to wait?  
A good answer uses concrete sensory details that collectively evoke tension. A poor answer uses abstract words ("scary place", "bad feeling") without sensory grounding, showing the student cannot construct atmosphere through setting.
